opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the history of engineering in general gives us a pretty strong hint here. The first airplane wasn't the most elegant possible flying machine, and the first computers were these huge, kludgy assemblages of vacuum tubes. Usually the first version of any really complex technology is a somewhat messy combination of different components, and only later, once you understand what's going on, do you find the cleaner and simpler formulation.

With intelligence specifically, I think there's a deeper reason too. General intelligence, at least the kind of human-like general intelligence we're aiming at, has to deal with a whole bunch of different kinds of problems under limited computational resources. In the abstract you can write down very simple, elegant formulations of general intelligence. Marcus Hutter's AIXI is a beautiful mathematical theory, but it requires effectively infinite computing power. Once you constrain yourself to a real system with finite memory and processing, you have to exploit the specific structure of the environment you're in: space, time, other agents, language, cause and effect. Each kind of structure tends to call for somewhat specialized learning and reasoning mechanisms.

If you look at the human brain, it's not one simple algorithm repeated everywhere. You've got the cortex, the hippocampus, the basal ganglia, the cerebellum, all these different subsystems with different architectures that evolved to do different things and then learned to cooperate. Evolution is a tinkerer, not an elegant designer, and what came out works but is not pretty.

So my view, which has driven the work on OpenCog and now Hyperon, is that the most practical route to AGI is a cognitive architecture where multiple learning and reasoning algorithms—probabilistic logic, evolutionary learning, neural pattern recognition, attention allocation and so on—work together on a common knowledge representation and help each other out of their respective bottlenecks. I call that cognitive synergy. It's not as aesthetically satisfying as "just scale up one algorithm," and of course the deep learning folks have gotten amazingly far by scaling up. But I suspect that to get to genuine general intelligence, with real abstraction, reasoning and creativity, you'll need that kind of hybrid integration.

And then, once you have a working AGI, it can probably help us discover the elegant underlying theory, which would be a very nice outcome. But I'd be surprised if we get the elegant theory first and build from that.

r001.rationale: It describes early technologies as messy combinations of components, but does not explain that their form reflects the resources available to their creators.

r002.rationale: It says the first version is often messy and cleaner, simpler formulations emerge later, after people understand the technology better.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's partly a matter of looking at the one example of general intelligence we actually have, which is the human brain, and the human brain is not simple or elegant. It's a mess. It's a bunch of different subsystems that evolved at different times for different purposes, all kludged together and interacting in complicated ways. There's a hippocampus doing one kind of thing, a cerebellum doing something else, a neocortex that's quite different in structure from the older parts, and you have all these different neurotransmitter systems modulating things in ways we barely understand. Evolution didn't find a single elegant algorithm for intelligence. It found a lot of hacks that happen to work together.

Now, you could say, okay, evolution is a dumb search process, and human engineers could do better and find the elegant principle underlying all of it. And I'm sympathetic to that in the abstract. There may well be some deep mathematical theory of general intelligence. Something like Marcus Hutter's AIXI points in that direction, where you have a beautiful, compact formulation of what an optimal general agent would do. But AIXI is uncomputable, and even the approximations to it are wildly impractical given the kinds of resources we actually have. When you take an elegant theory and try to make it run in finite time and finite memory in a real world full of structured regularities, you end up adding special cases and heuristics and separate modules for perception, memory, planning, language, and so on. The elegance gets lost in the engineering.

And I think the reason for that is that general intelligence, in the practical sense we care about, isn't really about handling arbitrary problems optimally. It's about handling the particular kinds of problems that come up in the kind of world we live in, with the kinds of bodies and societies and timescales we have. That world has a lot of specific structure, and an efficient intelligence has to be shaped to exploit that structure. So you end up with a lot of different kinds of knowledge representation and learning that are good for different things. Deep neural nets are great for perception and pattern recognition. Logic-based systems are good at precise reasoning and abstraction. Evolutionary methods are good at creative search. You probably want some kind of attention allocation or economic mechanism to decide what the system should be thinking about. None of those on its own looks like it'll get you all the way there.

That's basically the bet I've been making with OpenCog for a long time, that the first AGI will be some kind of integrative, hybrid architecture, where you have multiple components that are each good at something, and the real work is in getting them to interoperate and cooperate on a common representation of the world. That's messier and less satisfying intellectually than a single elegant learning algorithm. But I think it's more likely to be how it actually gets done, and then after the fact, maybe we'll understand it well enough to derive the elegant theory that explains why it worked. Historically that's often how it goes. The engineering comes first and the beautiful theory comes afterward.

r001.rationale: The response describes intelligence as a mix of components shaped by evolution and practical constraints, but does not say inventions take form by cobbling together resources available to their creators.

r002.rationale: It says engineering comes first and that a beautiful theory may be derived afterward, clearly conveying that elegance can emerge after initial development.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think there may be a simple, elegant theory of general intelligence, but that doesn’t mean the first system we build will be a simple, elegant implementation of that theory. Those are different things.

We’re trying to make something work before we fully understand the principles behind it. In that situation, you tend to combine a bunch of mechanisms: something for learning from perception, something for reasoning, something for memory, something for deciding what to do. And then you figure out how to get those mechanisms to cooperate. There may be a deeper mathematical framework that unifies them, but you don’t necessarily have to discover it before you can build a working system.

Also, general intelligence in the abstract is different from intelligence that has to operate with limited resources in the world we inhabit. You can have a very compact description of a learning procedure that would work if you gave it an absurd amount of computation. Making it practical introduces structure and complexity.

So I wouldn’t rule out a beautiful, simple breakthrough. I just don’t see why we should expect that to come first. My expectation is that we’ll build something somewhat messy that works, and understanding why it works will help us find the more elegant formulation.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes combining mechanisms to make a system work, but does not explain that an invention’s form is shaped by the resources available to its creators.

r002.rationale: It expects an initially messy working system and says understanding it afterward can help reveal a more elegant formulation.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I’d distinguish between a simple principle that explains intelligence and a simple recipe for building an intelligent system. There might be some very elegant mathematical way to characterize what intelligence is, but that doesn’t mean you can turn it into a practical AGI with one short algorithm and a lot of computing power.

If you look at the human mind, we have all these different kinds of memory, learning, reasoning, perception, motivation, and so forth. They’re doing different things, but they’re also helping each other. When one way of solving a problem gets stuck, another can step in. My intuition is that you need something of that sort—multiple processes interacting in the right way—to get general intelligence working with realistic computational resources.

Now, that doesn’t mean we have to reproduce every messy detail of the brain. Evolution certainly wasn’t optimizing for elegant software design. But I suspect the first AGI will be a somewhat complicated system whose components have been made to work together through a mixture of theory and experimentation. Once we understand why it works, we may be able to simplify it tremendously. The beautiful, elegant formulation may come after the first working system.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the first AGI may combine interacting processes and be shaped by theory and experimentation, but it does not explain that early inventions take form by cobbling together the resources available to their creators.

r002.rationale: The candidate says the first working system may be somewhat complicated and that it may be simplified once its workings are understood, so elegance can come after initial development.
